metadata.title: What do university students know about Artificial Intelligence? Development and validation of an AI literacy test

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study used a voluntary web-based survey of German-speaking university students recruited from six universities in southern Germany, with exclusions for missingness in the AI literacy test and for implausibly fast completion. The paper does not report the use of complex survey sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures, and the analysis is based on Item Response Theory (IRT) rather than ILSA-style PV estimation. Because no ILSA sampling frame or weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) are described, student weights are treated as not reported. The main data preparation steps explicitly include excluding 44 invalid cases (more than 25% missing AI literacy responses; completion time <4 minutes) and removing one poorly discriminating item (item 07) after initial 3-PL estimation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values (PVs) are not applicable because the dependent variable is an AI literacy knowledge test analyzed via Item Response Theory (IRT) models (Rasch/2-PL/3-PL) rather than PV-based cognitive achievement scores from an ILSA program. Missing-data handling is implemented through case exclusion: participants with more than 25% missing values in the AI literacy test were removed before analysis, which corresponds to listwise deletion for the analytic sample. The paper does not describe any PV-based imputation because PVs are not part of the measurement approach used here.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Validation study sample comprised German-speaking university students recruited from six universities in southern Germany via email invitation to a voluntary web-based study. From 1330 participants, 44 invalid cases were excluded: 4 participants were excluded for having more than 25% missing values in the AI literacy test, and 40 participants were excluded for completing the survey too quickly (less than 4 minutes; median completion time reported as 16.63). The final analytic sample size was N=1286. For the measurement model, item 07 was eliminated due to a distinctly poor discrimination parameter (a=0.093), and the remaining 30 items were used for subsequent person-ability estimation.

main_findings.dataset_used: AI literacy test validation (German university students; 6 universities; web-based pilot/validation)
main_findings.performance_metrics: IRT model selection: 3-PL best by AIC/BIC and fit indices (M2=815.5581, RMSEA=0.026, SRMR=0.039, TLI=0.964, CFI=0.966). Reliability: EAP reliability r=0.85; Cronbach’s alpha α=0.82. Validity correlations (IRT scores): AI literacy with self-efficacy r=0.39 (p<.001), interest r=0.36 (p<.001), positive attitude r=0.27 (p<.001), negative attitude r=-0.26 (p<.001). Discrimination: item 07 eliminated due to a=0.093. Additional analysis (Discrimination of low vs high AI literacy (group differences by prior AI experience)): Group differences: students who had taken AI courses scored higher (M=0.711, SD=0.797) than those who had not (M=-0.166, SD=0.849), t(396.8)=15.359, p<.001, d=1.044. Informal learning frequency: F(6,1267)=26.63, p<.001, η2=0.112. Prior computer science study: M=0.416 (SD=0.951) vs M=-0.074 (SD=0.878), t(275.03)=6.847, p<.001, d=0.551. Discipline comparison: engineering highest, then STEM, then social sciences; only engineering vs social sciences difference significant (p<.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the AI literacy test validation data from German university students, the study leveraged AI self-efficacy, interest in AI, attitudes toward AI, and prior computer science study to estimate AI literacy knowledge via a 3-PL IRT model, finding that AI literacy showed significant positive associations with self-efficacy, interest, and positive attitude and a significant negative association with negative attitude. This indicates that universities should pair AI course content with motivational and attitudinal supports (e.g., building confidence and interest) to improve students’ AI literacy, while recognizing that the study is correlational and not causal.

data.outcome_summary: The paper develops and validates a theory-based AI literacy knowledge test for German university students using a 30-item multiple-choice instrument plus a sorting task (steps of machine learning). The validation sample comprised N=1286 students recruited from six universities in southern Germany, after excluding 44 invalid cases (high missingness in the AI literacy test and implausibly fast completion). Measurement was analyzed with IRT, comparing Rasch, 2-PL, and 3-PL models; the 3-PL model showed the best fit (M2=815.5581, RMSEA=0.026, SRMR=0.039, TLI=0.964, CFI=0.966) and acceptable reliability (EAP r=0.85; Cronbach’s α=0.82). Validity evidence included significant correlations with AI self-efficacy, interest, and attitudes, and group differences by prior AI learning and discipline. Limitations include voluntary sampling and correlational validity evidence rather than causal inference.
